name: Zopiclone (Imovane)
summary: Short-term prescription sleep medication used for insomnia (trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early). Works fast, but next-day grogginess, dependence, and dangerous sleep behaviors are real risks—especially if you mix it with alcohol, opioids, or take it without a full night to sleep.
description: Zopiclone is a non-benzodiazepine hypnotic (“Z-drug”) that helps you fall asleep faster, sleep longer, and wake up less during the night. It should be taken right before bed, only when you can get a full night of sleep. It’s meant for short-term use; if you’re needing it beyond a few weeks, that’s a sign to step back and address the underlying insomnia drivers (CBT-I, anxiety, depression, substances, sleep apnea, meds). It can cause next-day impairment, memory gaps, and rare but serious complex sleep behaviors like sleep-walking or sleep-driving—stop it immediately if that happens.
patient_summary: Zopiclone is a fast-onset sleep medication for short-term insomnia. Take it right before bed only if you can sleep a full night. It can cause a bitter taste, grogginess, dizziness, and memory gaps—and in rare cases, dangerous “complex sleep behaviors” like sleep-walking or sleep-driving. Avoid alcohol and opioids. Don’t use long-term unless benefits clearly outweigh risks and non-med options aren’t working.

linked_conditions.context: Short-term symptomatic relief of insomnia when sleep is disrupted by difficulty falling asleep, frequent awakenings, and/or early-morning awakenings. Best used as a time-limited tool while CBT-I and the root cause of insomnia are addressed.
Not an anxiety treatment. But if anxiety is driving insomnia, short-term bedtime use may reduce nighttime arousal while core treatment (CBT, SSRIs/SNRIs, sleep work) ramps up.
Use with caution. Worsening depression and suicidal thoughts have been reported with hypnotics in patients with or without depression; prescribe the smallest amount needed.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to zopiclone or any component of the formulation
Severe respiratory impairment (including significant sleep apnea syndrome)
History of complex sleep behaviors after taking any nonbenzodiazepine sedative/hypnotic

efficacy_response.patient_text: Zopiclone can help you fall asleep faster, wake up less during the night, and sleep longer. The trade-off is next-day impairment risk—so the goal is the lowest effective dose for the shortest time while you build durable sleep skills (CBT-I).

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP3A4 (major) and CYP2C8 (minor); metabolites have minimal or no activity

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Zopiclone is a prescription sleep medication used for short-term relief of {link:condition:insomnia:insomnia}. It’s meant for nights when sleep is disrupted by difficulty falling asleep, waking up repeatedly, or waking up too early. It’s not a long-term fix—if you’re still needing it after a few weeks, that’s a sign the real insomnia drivers need a full workup and a CBT-I plan.
items: {link:condition:insomnia:Insomnia (sleep maintenance)}: Waking up during the night and struggling to fall back asleep
{link:condition:insomnia:Early morning awakenings}: Waking up too early and not being able to return to sleep
Short-term bridge: Temporary support while you implement CBT-I and treat underlying causes (anxiety, depression, substances, circadian disruption, sleep apnea, restless legs, medication effects)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: People’s sleep meds stories are all over the map, but these themes show up a lot:

quotes: It shuts my brain up enough to actually fall asleep.
I’m not knocked out—I just stop hovering in that half-awake spiral.
If I take it and stay up, I get weird and foggy. Bed means bed.
I still wake up, but I’m more likely to fall back asleep.
It helps… but if my anxiety is high, it’s not magic.
The sleep was better, but the morning felt heavy.
I’m functional—but slower, like my reaction time is on delay.
If I didn’t get a full night, I paid for it the next day.
items.note: Next-day driving and work performance can be impaired—especially at higher doses or if you don’t get a full night of sleep.

quotes: I woke up with dry mouth and a gross taste that wouldn’t quit.
It works, but the taste makes me regret it a little.
items.note: Dysgeusia (bitter/metallic taste) is one of the most “classic” complaints with zopiclone.

quotes: I didn’t remember sending those texts.
I felt kind of intoxicated and then… blank.
If anything sleep-walky happens, I’m done with it.
items.note: Rare but serious: complex sleep behaviors (sleep-walking, sleep-driving, doing things while not fully awake). Stop the med immediately and contact your prescriber if this happens.

quotes: After a while it didn’t hit the same.
Stopping made my sleep rebound hard for a couple nights.
I realized I was relying on it instead of fixing my sleep.
items.note: Dependence and withdrawal can happen, especially with higher doses or longer use. That’s why this is meant to be short-term.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Zopiclone has a fast onset—so timing matters. Take it right before bed (or only once you’re already in bed), and only if you can sleep a full night.
key_points: Rapid onset: Take immediately before bedtime (don’t take it and then do chores)
<2 hours: Peak blood levels in most adults
~5 hours: Average half-life (elderly ~7 hours; hepatic impairment ~12 hours)
Up to ~11 hours: Driving and next-day performance impairment has been reported—risk is higher at higher doses or if you don’t get a full night of sleep
Best practice: Plan at least a full night of sleep and wait at least 12 hours before high-alert activities if you feel any residual effects

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Zopiclone can reduce how long it takes to fall asleep, increase total sleep time, and reduce awakenings. The main limitation is that benefits are often modest, while risks (next-day impairment, dependence, abnormal behaviors) can be meaningful. That’s why this medication is best treated like a short-term tool, not your long-term sleep plan.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: If you’ve ever had sleep-walking, sleep-driving, or doing things in your sleep after a sedative-hypnotic: zopiclone is a no-go. And never mix this with alcohol or opioids.
sections.black_box: [Canadian Boxed Warning]: Zopiclone can cause complex sleep behaviors (including sleep-walking and sleep-driving) that may result in serious injuries or death. Zopiclone can also cause addiction, abuse, and misuse, and severe or life-threatening withdrawal. Concomitant use with opioids may cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death.
other: Next-day impairment: Mental and physical performance can be impaired the next day—risk increases with higher doses, short sleep time, and other sedatives
Anterograde amnesia: Memory gaps can occur; don’t take it unless a full night of sleep is possible
Abnormal thinking/behavior: Agitation, aggression, hallucinations, disinhibition can occur unpredictably
Depression/suicidality: Worsening depression and suicidal ideation/attempts have been reported with hypnotics; prescribe the smallest amount needed
Respiratory disease: Use caution in chronic respiratory disease; contraindicated in severe respiratory impairment (including significant sleep apnea)
Hepatic impairment: Dose reduce in mild-to-moderate impairment; contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment
Fall risk: Especially in older adults or anyone at risk for falls
patient_counseling: Take it right before bed (or only once you’re already in bed). Don’t “take it early” and hope it kicks in later.
Do not use alcohol with this medication. Not “maybe.” Not “just one.” Just no.
Avoid opioids and other sedatives unless your prescriber explicitly plans it and monitors you closely.
Do not drive, operate machinery, or do high-risk tasks if you feel groggy, slowed, or “off.”
If you do anything unusual in your sleep (sleep-walking, sleep-driving, eating, phone calls, sex) or you don’t remember the night: stop the medication and contact your prescriber immediately.
If you’ve been taking it regularly, don’t stop abruptly—taper to reduce rebound insomnia and withdrawal risk.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common themes: bitter/metallic taste, next-day sedation, dizziness/unsteadiness, and memory problems. Rare but serious: complex sleep behaviors and respiratory depression (especially with other sedatives).
plain_language_list: Bitter/metallic taste or bad breath (classic zopiclone complaint)
Daytime drowsiness or feeling “hungover” the next day
Memory gaps or confusion (especially if you don’t sleep a full night)

common.patient_note: This is one of the most recognizable side effects with zopiclone. It can show up quickly and can be annoying enough that people stop the medication even if sleep improves.

You can feel slowed, foggy, or less coordinated the next day—especially at higher doses, if you took it late, or if you didn’t get enough sleep. Driving impairment has been reported up to 11 hours after a dose.
Unsteadiness can look like mild intoxication. This is a big deal for anyone with fall risk—especially older adults.
You might not form clear memories after you take it. If you take it and stay up, the odds of weird behavior + memory gaps go up.

common.symptom: Mood and behavior changes (agitation, irritability, aggression, hallucinations)
common.patient_note: Most people don’t get this, but when it happens it can be intense and unpredictable. If you feel activated, aggressive, detached, or hallucinate—stop the medication and contact your prescriber.

serious: Complex sleep behaviors (sleep-walking, sleep-driving, sleep-eating, sleep-talking, somnambulism) with amnesia: can cause serious injury or death; discontinue immediately if this occurs
Respiratory depression (especially with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives): slow or shallow breathing, blue lips, unresponsiveness—medical emergency
Severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis, angioedema): facial swelling, throat tightness, trouble breathing—medical emergency
Dependence and withdrawal syndrome: rebound insomnia, anxiety, tremor, agitation; rarely seizures or delirium after abrupt discontinuation, especially after sustained use or higher doses
Worsening depression or suicidal ideation/attempts in susceptible patients

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Zopiclone is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4, so inhibitors can raise levels and increase next-day impairment. Anything that adds sedation (alcohol, opioids, other sleep meds) stacks risk fast.

items.risk: Additive CNS depression, profound sedation, respiratory depression, abnormal behaviors, severe impairment. Complex sleep behaviors can occur with or without alcohol—but alcohol increases overall risk.
[Canadian Boxed Warning]: Profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death.
items.action: Avoid whenever possible. If unavoidable, use minimum doses/duration and monitor closely for sedation and slowed breathing.

items.with: Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines, antipsychotics, muscle relaxants, gabapentinoids, cannabis)
items.risk: Stacked sedation, impaired coordination, falls, memory problems, respiratory suppression in high-risk scenarios.
items.action: Use caution, minimize combinations, and reassess if next-day impairment occurs.

items.risk: Can increase zopiclone effects/toxicity via CYP3A4 inhibition (more drowsiness, confusion, ataxia, respiratory depression).
items.action: Avoid grapefruit products. If exposure happens, stick to the lowest effective bedtime dose and monitor closely for toxicity.

items.with: Strong/moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (class effect: some macrolides, azoles, protease inhibitors)
items.risk: Higher zopiclone exposure and next-day impairment risk.
items.action: Consider avoidance or dose reduction; reassess sedation and driving risk.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been taking zopiclone regularly, don’t stop abruptly. The most common problem is rebound insomnia (your sleep briefly gets worse), but withdrawal symptoms can happen—especially at higher doses or longer use. A slow taper plus CBT-I is the cleanest exit strategy.
key_points: Typical taper: Reduce by ~25% of the original dose each week or every other week.
Practical step-down: Decrease by about 1.875 to 2.5 mg each week or every other week (depending on available tablet strengths).
If you’ve been on 7.5 mg nightly for a long time: taper even more slowly and pair with CBT-I to reduce rebound insomnia and relapse.
Watch for rebound insomnia for 1-2 days after dose reductions—plan for it and don’t panic-titrate upward.
Avoid alcohol and other sedatives during taper; they muddy the picture and raise risk.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Zopiclone is taken by mouth, right before bedtime. The goal is the lowest effective dose, used for the shortest time. If you can’t get a full night of sleep, skip it—next-day impairment risk jumps.

adult.sleep_initial: 3.75 mg PO once nightly at bedtime as needed
adult.sleep_titration: May increase to 5 mg or 7.5 mg at bedtime based on response and tolerability
adult.bedtime: Take immediately before bedtime (or only once you are already in bed) and only if a full night of sleep is possible
adult.prn_use: Use as needed for short-term insomnia; generally limit ongoing use beyond 7-10 nights, and limit long-term use (>4 weeks) to cases where nonpharmacologic options are not available or not effective and benefits outweigh risks

sections.simple_explanation: Think of zopiclone as a short-term sleep stabilizer, not a long-term sleep plan. It can help with falling asleep and staying asleep, but it can also leave you groggy or impaired the next day—especially if you take it late or don’t sleep long enough.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Zopiclone can cross the placenta and is present in breast milk. It may cause newborn sedation and withdrawal-like symptoms. Older adults are at higher risk for delirium, falls, fractures, and car crashes—so this is generally a med to avoid after 65.
sections.pregnancy: Zopiclone crosses the placenta. Human outcome data exist, but risk concerns are similar to benzodiazepines: possible congenital malformations with first-trimester exposure and neonatal CNS/respiratory depression and withdrawal symptoms with later exposure. The manufacturer does not recommend use during pregnancy; short-term use may be considered only in severe, intractable insomnia after careful risk-benefit discussion, with close newborn monitoring if exposure occurs.
sections.lactation: Zopiclone is present in breast milk and breast milk concentrations may be substantial relative to maternal plasma. The manufacturer does not recommend breastfeeding during zopiclone therapy. If exposure occurs, monitor the infant for sedation, feeding problems, hypotonia, and respiratory issues.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid use when possible. If used despite risks: start 3.75 mg at bedtime as needed and do not exceed 5 mg/day. Older adults are more sensitive to confusion, amnesia, falls, and next-day impairment; benefits on sleep are often modest while harms can be significant.
sections.hepatic: Mild-to-moderate hepatic impairment: Start 3.75 mg PO at bedtime; may cautiously increase up to 5 mg at bedtime if clinically indicated. Severe hepatic impairment: Contraindicated.
sections.renal: Labeling recommends a max of 5 mg/day in kidney impairment (exact eGFR threshold may not be specified in labeling). Practical approach: eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m2: no adjustment. eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2 (and dialysis/CRRT/PIRRT): start 3.75 mg at bedtime; may cautiously increase to 5 mg at bedtime if needed; max 5 mg/day due to higher next-day impairment risk.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Next-day impairment: morning grogginess, slowed reaction time, balance problems—especially after dose increases or if sleep time was shortened
Abnormal behaviors or thinking: agitation, aggression, hallucinations, disinhibition, confusion
Complex sleep behaviors: sleep-walking, sleep-driving, sleep-eating, phone calls, sex while not fully awake—stop immediately if this occurs
Respiratory status in higher-risk patients: chronic lung disease, suspected sleep apnea, or any sedative combinations (especially opioids)
Mood: worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, irritability—especially in patients with underlying mood disorders
Misuse/dependence signals: escalating dose, early refills, “can’t sleep at all without it,” combining with alcohol or other sedatives
Rebound insomnia and withdrawal symptoms during discontinuation: restlessness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia flare

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Zopiclone is available as oral tablets. Brands and excipients vary by manufacturer, so check product specifics if you have allergies or lactose intolerance concerns.
items: Imovane (Canada): 7.5 mg tablet (some formulations contain color additives)
Some formulations may contain lactose (avoid in galactose intolerance syndromes such as glucose-galactose malabsorption or galactosemia)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Zopiclone is a “Z-drug” that acts like a benzodiazepine-style sedative at the GABA-A receptor complex. In plain English: it turns up the brain’s braking system so the nervous system settles down enough for sleep—shorter time to fall asleep, fewer awakenings, and longer total sleep.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Zopiclone sits in the short-term insomnia toolbox. It can be helpful when you need rapid symptom relief, but it should not replace CBT-I or a real insomnia workup. If insomnia persists beyond 7-10 days (or you’re needing treatment beyond 2-3 consecutive weeks), that’s a signal to reassess for psychiatric drivers (anxiety, depression, trauma), substances (alcohol/cannabis), circadian issues, sleep apnea, restless legs, medication side effects, or environmental/schedule factors. Older adults (65+) are a special caution zone: Z-drugs act a lot like benzos in the real world—delirium, falls, fractures, car crashes—so avoidance is usually the right call.

seo.title: Zopiclone (Imovane): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects & Safe Tapering
seo.description: Zopiclone (Imovane) for short-term insomnia: bedtime dosing (3.75–7.5 mg), bitter taste, next-day impairment, complex sleep behaviors, dangerous mixing with alcohol/opioids, and how to taper safely.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Zopiclone is used for short-term relief of insomnia—trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up too early. It’s a symptom-relief tool, not a long-term sleep plan.

faqs.q: How do I take zopiclone правильно (the safest way)?
faqs.a: Take it by mouth immediately before bedtime (or only once you’re already in bed). Only take it if you can sleep a full night. Don’t take it and then stay up—this increases the chance of memory gaps, weird behavior, and next-day impairment.

faqs.q: What’s the typical zopiclone dose for insomnia?
faqs.a: Many adults start at 3.75 mg at bedtime as needed. If needed and tolerated, the dose may be increased to 5 mg or 7.5 mg at bedtime. The maximum adult dose is 7.5 mg/day at bedtime.

faqs.q: Why does zopiclone leave a bitter or metallic taste?
faqs.a: That bitter/metal taste (dysgeusia) is a known zopiclone side effect and one of the most common reasons people dislike it. It’s annoying but usually not dangerous.

faqs.q: Can zopiclone affect driving the next day?
faqs.a: Yes. Next-day impairment can happen—slower reaction time, grogginess, poor coordination—and driving performance may be affected hours after a dose, especially if you took a higher dose, took it late, or didn’t sleep long enough. If you feel even slightly impaired, don’t drive.

faqs.q: What are “complex sleep behaviors,” and how serious is that risk?
faqs.a: Complex sleep behaviors are things like sleep-walking, sleep-driving, eating, phone calls, or sex while not fully awake—often with no memory afterward. These events can cause serious injury or death. If this happens even once, stop zopiclone and contact your prescriber immediately.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with zopiclone?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol plus zopiclone is a bad combo—sedation and impairment stack fast, and it increases risk of dangerous behaviors and respiratory depression.

faqs.q: Is it safe to take zopiclone with opioids?
faqs.a: This combination is high risk. Concomitant use with opioids can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. It should be avoided whenever possible and only used with strict medical oversight if there are no alternatives.

faqs.q: How long should I use zopiclone?
faqs.a: Ideally, short-term. If insomnia doesn’t improve after 7–10 days, or if treatment is needed for more than 2–3 consecutive weeks, it’s time for a full reassessment (sleep apnea, anxiety/depression, substances, circadian issues, meds) and a CBT-I plan. Long-term use beyond 4 weeks should be rare and only when benefits clearly outweigh risks.

faqs.q: How do I stop zopiclone without rebound insomnia wrecking me?
faqs.a: If you’ve been using it regularly, taper instead of stopping abruptly. A common approach is reducing by about 25% of the original dose each week or every other week (often a step-down of ~1.875–2.5 mg per interval depending on tablet options). Pairing the taper with CBT-I makes the landing much smoother.

faqs.q: Is zopiclone okay for older adults (65+)?
faqs.a: Usually not. In older adults, Z-drugs are linked to delirium, falls, fractures, ER visits, hospitalizations, and motor vehicle crashes, while the actual sleep benefit is often small. If it’s used despite that, doses should be lower and capped (often max 5 mg/day), with close monitoring.

faqs.q: Is zopiclone safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: It’s generally not recommended. Zopiclone crosses the placenta and is found in breast milk. Exposure can lead to newborn sedation, breathing problems, feeding difficulties, hypotonia, and withdrawal-like symptoms. Short-term use may be considered only in severe, intractable insomnia after careful risk-benefit discussion with your clinician.
